entries.agreement: plural verb — the cacti are blooming
entries.variants: cacti (commoner in writing) · cactuses (commoner in speech)
entries.contrast: Both plurals are fully correct. Cacti sounds more botanical; cactuses sounds more casual, and neither will be marked wrong.

examples: He's treating a fungus on his foot.

entries.countability: countable, and uncountable in the mass sense
entries.agreement: plural verb — these fungi are edible
entries.variants: fungi is standard in science and general use; funguses is rare
entries.contrast: Two pronunciations of the plural coexist in American English — FUN-jy and FUN-gy — and both are accepted. The adjective is fungal.

senses.head: The central core of a group or plan
examples: Those four players formed the nucleus of the team.

entries.variants: nuclei is standard in every technical field
entries.contrast: Americans say /ˈnuːkliəs/, without the /j/ of British NYOO-. The adjective is nuclear — famously mispronounced ✗ NOO-kyuh-lur instead of NOO-klee-ur.

entries.meaning: The distance from the center of a circle to its edge; also a bone in the forearm.

examples: Measure the radius of the circle.
The two radii meet at the center.

senses.head: A surrounding area
body: Very common in everyday use. (радиус, округа)
examples: There's no gas station within a ten-mile radius.

senses.head: The forearm bone
examples: She fractured her radius in the fall.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the radii are equal
entries.variants: radii in mathematics; radiuses occasionally elsewhere
entries.contrast: Note the double i in radii — the stem ends in i and the plural adds another. Same in genii. The word is also a bone in the forearm, with the same plural.

examples: He is an alumnus of the same program.

senses.head: Informally — alum
body: Sex-neutral and increasingly standard in American usage. (выпускник, выпускница)
examples: Two alums now run the company.

senses.head: Extended to any former member
body: Of a company, team, or show. (бывший участник)
examples: The show's alumni include three future stars.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the alumni were invited
entries.variants: alumnus (one man) · alumna (one woman) · alumni (men, or a mixed group) · alumnae (women only) · alum / alums (informal, sex-neutral)
entries.contrast: This word has a full Latin gender system that English kept, and it trips everybody. Note especially that ✗ an alumni is wrong for one person — say an alumnus, an alumna, or informally an alum. Mixed groups take alumni.

entries.contrast: The Latin form is actually the result of a copying error in a Renaissance text, so the -i plural has no ancient authority — which has not stopped it from becoming standard.

examples: An octopus escaped through a two-inch gap.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the octopuses were moved to a larger tank
entries.variants: octopuses is standard; octopi is common but has no basis; octopodes is technically correct and sounds absurd
entries.contrast: ✗ Octopi is the most confidently mispronounced plural in English. The word is Greek, so the Latin -us → -i rule never applied to it. If you want the historical plural it is octopodes; if you want to be understood, say octopuses.

senses.head: The infectious agent
examples: The virus spreads through the air.
Several viruses circulate every winter.

examples: His laptop picked up a virus.

senses.head: Figuratively — something that spreads

entries.agreement: plural verb — these viruses mutate quickly
entries.contrast: ✗ Viri and ✗ virii are both wrong and always have been. In Latin virus was a mass noun meaning 'poison' and had no plural at all, so English simply made a regular one. The same goes for campus → campuses, bonus → bonuses, status → statuses, census → censuses.

entries.agreement: plural verb — these genera are closely related
entries.contrast: Note the vowel shift: singular JEE-nuhs, plural JEN-ur-uh. Not ✗ genuses in scientific writing, and never ✗ geni. In classification a genus sits above a species.
